turns.speaker: SPEAKER_00
turns.text: Let's review the migration of the payment orchestration layer from the monolith to the distributed architecture. The main constraint is that we cannot introduce duplicate charges while we move traffic gradually.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_01
turns.text: The current design has the checkout service calling the payment gateway adapter synchronously. In the new design, checkout publishes a PaymentRequested event to Kafka, and the orchestration service consumes it.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_02
turns.text: For ordering, we are using Kafka partitions keyed by payment_id. That gives us ordering for events with the same key, but it does not give global ordering across all payments.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_03
turns.text: The consumer group will run three replicas initially. We should not assume that three replicas means three active leaders, because Kafka assigns partitions and only one consumer in the group owns a partition at a time.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_00
turns.text: For the database, the ledger remains on PostgreSQL. We are using serializable transactions only around the balance mutation, not around the entire request lifecycle.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_01
turns.text: The idempotency table is keyed by merchant_id and idempotency_key. The STT system wrote this as item potency table in one place, but the actual identifier is idempotency_key.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_02
turns.text: We also have a unique constraint on merchant_id, idempotency_key, and operation_type. If a retry arrives with the same key and a different amount, we reject it instead of silently updating the original request.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_03
turns.text: For the cache, Redis is only an optimization. We must not treat a Redis hit as proof that a payment exists in the ledger, because cache eviction or failover can remove that entry.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_00
turns.text: The deployment target is cube net ease on three availability zones. The namespace is payments-prod, and the service account is payment-orchestrator.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_01
turns.text: For service-to-service calls, we are standardizing on G R P C with protobuf. The public API remains REST under /api/v2/payments, so clients do not need to know about the internal transport.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_02
turns.text: The gRPC method is ProcessPayment, and the protobuf package is payments.v2. We should preserve the field name payment_id because downstream consumers already depend on it.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_03
turns.text: For consensus inside the configuration service, we use E T C D. The leader election timeout is 1000 milliseconds and the heartbeat interval is 100 milliseconds.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_00
turns.text: The rough algorithm is only relevant to the metadata cluster, not the payment ledger. I want that distinction in the documentation because people keep mixing the two consistency mechanisms.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_01
turns.text: Right, and the metadata cluster has five nodes. Losing two nodes is tolerated, but if we lose three, the cluster cannot maintain quorum and writes stop.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_02
turns.text: On observability, promise us is scraping the application metrics and Grafana is rendering the dashboards. The scrape interval is 15 seconds.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_03
turns.text: We are also adding OpenTelemetry tracing. Trace IDs must propagate through the Kafka headers so that checkout, orchestration, and the gateway can be correlated.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_00
turns.text: The alert should fire if payment processing p95 exceeds 800 milliseconds for 10 minutes, but I am not proposing that as a final SLO yet.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_01
turns.text: The current p95 is 420 milliseconds and p99 is 1.8 seconds. We should not optimize only for p95 because the tail latency is where the customer-visible timeouts happen.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_02
turns.text: There is another issue with retries. The gateway uses exponential backoff with a maximum of 30 seconds, while our Kafka consumer retry policy currently allows 5 attempts.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_03
turns.text: If the gateway times out after sending the authorization request, we cannot assume the authorization failed. The next retry has to query the provider or use the idempotency key.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_00
turns.text: Exactly. A timeout is not a negative acknowledgment. The provider may have accepted the transaction even though our HTTP client never received the response.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_01
turns.text: For the state machine, CREATED moves to AUTHORIZING, then AUTHORIZED or DECLINED. An AUTHORIZED payment can move to CAPTURED, but a DECLINED payment cannot move directly to CAPTURED.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_02
turns.text: Refunds are separate from the authorization state machine. The refund endpoint is POST /api/v2/refunds, and the request includes original_payment_id and refund_amount.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_03
turns.text: There is a concurrency edge case when a capture and a refund arrive nearly simultaneously. PostgreSQL row locking should serialize the ledger mutation, but we need an integration test to prove the invariant.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_00
turns.text: I can write that integration test this week. I am not committing to Friday because the provider sandbox has been unstable.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_01
turns.text: The provider sandbox returned HTTP 409 twice yesterday. That is different from HTTP 429, which indicates rate limiting.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_02
turns.text: We also saw one HTTP 500 from the provider, but we don't know whether it represents a transient provider failure or a malformed request on our side.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_03
turns.text: For security, Open I D Connect will be used between the admin portal and the identity provider. Access tokens should have a 15 minute lifetime.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_00
turns.text: The admin portal must not receive the provider client secret. That secret stays in the backend secret store and is injected only into the authentication service.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_01
turns.text: For deployment, we can use a rolling update with maxUnavailable set to 0 and maxSurge set to 1. That is a proposal, not a final deployment decision.

turns.text: If the canary stays below 0.5 percent error rate for 30 minutes, we could increase traffic from 5 percent to 25 percent. Again, this is a proposed rollout policy.

turns.text: The final rollout threshold has not been approved yet. Priya owns the release checklist, and Arjun owns the database migration script.

turns.text: One STT error worth checking is graf on a dashboards. The actual product name in the architecture is Grafana, but if someone says the phrase graph on a dashboard in ordinary English, that should not automatically become Grafana.

turns.text: There is a 2 GB Kafka topic retention setting in staging and 14 days in production. We are considering 30 days for production, but that is not approved.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_01
turns.text: For load testing, the target is 1,240 requests per second with 40 percent reads and 60 percent writes. The test duration is 20 minutes.

turns.speaker: SPEAKER_03
